services.name: Drain Cleaning
services.h1: Drain Cleaning in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Drain Cleaning | BT Round Rock Plumbing | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: BT Round Rock Plumbing clears slow, clogged, and backed-up drains in Round Rock, TX. Tell us which fixture is affected and where water is standing.
services.blurb: We clear slow sinks, backed-up tubs, and blocked drains across Round Rock.

paragraphs: A sink that gurgles after the faucet shuts off, a tub that holds water around your feet, or a floor drain with a sewer smell usually points to buildup somewhere past the fixture opening. Water may drain slowly for days before grease, soap residue, hair, or food scraps close off enough of the pipe to stop it completely. A kitchen sink can also back up into the other bowl when the shared branch line cannot carry water away.

We check the fixture drain, trap, branch pipe, and accessible cleanout to locate the blockage rather than treating every slow drain as the same problem. We cover drain cleaning calls in Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch, including sinks, tubs, showers, and floor drains. A drain that only slows can be scheduled before it stops, but water rising in a sink, tub, or floor drain should not wait because the blockage can overflow into cabinets, flooring, or the next connected fixture.

sections.heading: Gurgling sinks and standing water
paragraphs: Customers often call about a kitchen sink that fills while the dishwasher drains, a bathroom basin that empties slowly, or a shower pan that leaves a ring of water after use. A tub may bubble at the drain while the nearby toilet flushes, which can mean water is meeting resistance in a shared branch pipe. Some callers notice a rotten sewer smell from a floor drain, while others find black water coming up through a shower drain or laundry standpipe.

A sink stopper packed with hair, a trap holding grease, and a blockage farther down a drain line can all make the same fixture drain slowly. Gurgling can also come from a partial obstruction that pulls air through the trap as water moves past it. These symptoms sound similar over the phone, but the fixture, pipe route, and location of the buildup call for different labor and equipment, which is why we inspect before defining the work.

sections.heading: Drain inspection and cable run
paragraphs: We begin the callout by asking which fixture backs up first, running water at the affected drain, and checking whether another sink, tub, or floor drain reacts. We remove the stopper or trap when access allows, inspect the visible pipe for buildup, and look for an accessible cleanout on the branch or main line. Kitchen and bathroom drain pipes commonly measure from 1 1/2 to 2 inches across, so we match the cable and cutting head to the opening and pipe size. We also note the route from the fixture to the cleanout, especially where a cabinet, crawlspace, or wall limits access.

A stopper cleaning or trap check may take 15 to 30 minutes, while a cable run through an accessible branch drain commonly takes 30 to 90 minutes depending on the pipe route and material in the line. During the same visit, we clear reachable buildup, flush the fixture repeatedly, and check that the trap and drain connection reseal correctly. We refit the trap and replace a worn slip-joint washer only if it will not seal after reassembly. A blockage beyond the accessible cleanout, a damaged pipe, or a line that needs further investigation may require a return visit after we establish where the obstruction sits.

sections.heading: Cleanouts, pipe route, and buildup
paragraphs: A capped cleanout near the fixture, outside wall, or yard gives us a direct route into the drain pipe and usually reduces the amount of cabinet or fixture access needed. A cleanout hidden behind shelving, a tight vanity, or finished wall material adds setup and removal work before a cable can enter the line. The route also matters: a short bathroom branch differs from a drain pipe that travels under a slab or across a long section of the house.

Hair and soap residue near a shower trap often clear differently from hardened grease in a kitchen branch or roots entering an exterior line. A removable trap under a sink gives us one access point, while a toilet, floor drain, or concealed pipe may require a different entry route. If cleaning reveals a broken section, recurring root entry, or work that moves beyond the drain opening, the pipe condition and any required approval can change the scope from a straightforward clearing to follow-up work.

sections.heading: Fixture and cleanout location
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room and fixture has the problem, whether it is the kitchen sink, shower, tub, bathroom basin, or floor drain. Tell us whether water is standing now, whether another fixture makes it bubble, and whether the backup appeared after using the dishwasher, washing machine, or garbage disposal. If you can safely see a capped cleanout pipe in a cabinet, garage, yard, or crawlspace, let us know where it sits.

A photo of the sink cabinet, trap, disposal, or floor drain can show the access around the pipe before we arrive. Mention any drain cleaner already poured into the fixture so we can handle the trap and standing water safely. Call BT Round Rock Plumbing at (737) 215-4933 before standing water reaches a cabinet base, shower pan edge, or floor surface and turns a blocked drain into an overflow cleanup.

services.name: Water Heater Repair
services.h1: Water Heater Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Water Heater Repair Round Rock, TX | BT Round Rock Plumbing
services.meta: BT Round Rock Plumbing handles water heater repair in Round Rock, TX, including no hot water, leaks, pilot faults, and temperature control problems.
services.blurb: Water heater repairs for no hot water, leaks, noises, and pilot faults.

paragraphs: No hot water at every faucet and water collecting beneath a heater often get called the same problem, but they lead us to different parts of the unit. From the hallway, a dry utility closet while every shower and sink runs cold points toward the burner, element, thermostat, or power supply; water crossing the closet threshold points toward a tank, valve, fitting, or drain connection. We handle both water heater faults in Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch.

A heater that stays cold but holds water can usually wait for a planned repair, although a gas smell, burning odor, or tripped breaker changes that assessment. A steady puddle, a wet platform, or water running from the tank jacket should not wait because water can spread into drywall, flooring, and the framing around the closet. We isolate the water source, test the heater components, and repair the part that caused the loss of hot water or the leak.

sections.heading: No hot water or puddle
paragraphs: “No hot water” may mean the water stays cold at every fixture, or it may mean a shower turns cold after only a short run. A popping or rumbling sound from the tank can follow sediment buildup around the burner or lower element. A puddle under the heater, rust-colored water at a hot tap, or moisture at the temperature-and-pressure relief valve points us toward a different set of parts.

Gas water heaters can also stop heating after a pilot goes out, a thermocouple fails, or the burner does not receive gas. Electric models may lose one heating element and still produce a small amount of warm water before going cold. These calls can sound alike from the kitchen or bathroom, but the tank, valve, burner, element, and control each require separate work and carry different parts requirements.

sections.heading: Water heater inspection
paragraphs: We start the callout by checking the model plate, tank capacity, fuel type, shutoff valves, drain connection, and the floor around the heater. On an electric unit, we test the disconnect, thermostat, and elements at the access panels; on a gas unit, we inspect the pilot, igniter, burner, vent pipe, and gas control. We also check water temperature and inspect the relief valve, which opens at about 150 psi or 210°F when it operates correctly.

A straightforward inspection and component test commonly takes 30 to 60 minutes, depending on whether the heater sits in a closet, attic, garage, or cabinet. We can often replace a thermostat, heating element, pilot component, relief valve, or supply connector during the same visit if the correct part is available and the shutoff works. A leaking tank, inaccessible vent connection, replacement heater, or ordered control valve usually calls for a return appointment after we confirm the model and installation requirements.

sections.heading: Shutoff valves and access
paragraphs: The age and condition of the heater matter because a newer tank with a failed element or gas control can make sense to repair, while corrosion around the tank seam changes the scope of the work. A model plate and serial number help identify the correct thermostat, element, burner assembly, anode rod, or control valve. Parts that are discontinued or specific to a tankless unit may need to be ordered rather than fitted from standard stock.

Access also moves the work involved. A heater behind a narrow closet door, above a ceiling opening, or in an attic may require more time around the drain pan, vent pipe, water lines, and flooring. A seized cold-water shutoff can add work before we can safely remove a valve or disconnect the heater, and a replacement installation may require permit or inspection sign-off depending on the location and work involved.

sections.heading: Model plate and closet access
paragraphs: Before calling, check the model number and serial number on the manufacturer plate, usually attached to the side of the tank or behind a front panel on some tankless units. Note whether the heater sits in a garage, utility closet, attic, or cabinet, and whether a puddle is present at the base, relief valve, or pipe above it. If hot water still runs, tell us whether every faucet stays cold or whether the temperature drops only after several minutes.

A photo of the plate, the shutoff valve, and the space in front of the heater helps us identify likely parts and plan access. Keep the area around the tank clear, but do not remove an electrical panel or relight a pilot if you smell gas. Call BT Round Rock Plumbing at (737) 215-4933 before a leaking tank spreads water into the closet floor, wallboard, or adjacent room.

services.name: Leak Repair
services.h1: Leak Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Leak Repair | BT Round Rock Plumbing | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: BT Round Rock Plumbing handles leak repair in Round Rock, TX, locating water loss at pipes, valves, fixtures, and hidden connections.
services.blurb: We locate and repair leaking pipes, valves, fittings, and fixture connections.

paragraphs: A drip under the kitchen sink can soak the cabinet floor slowly, then swell the particleboard around the supply valves and trap. A damp spot on a ceiling can spread beyond the pipe opening as water follows framing, insulation, and drywall. After a week or a month, a small leak may leave staining, peeling paint, warped flooring, or mold growth behind a wall.

We trace the water to the fitting, pipe, valve, or fixture connection that has failed instead of treating the visible stain as the source. A leak from an exposed compression nut may stay contained for a while, but a leak inside a wall, under a slab, or beneath a toilet needs attention sooner because water can keep moving through building materials. Leak repair should not wait when water is actively running, pooling, or reaching drywall, cabinets, flooring, or electrical fixtures.

sections.heading: Water stains and dripping pipes
paragraphs: Customers often call us about a brown ceiling spot, a pipe that keeps dripping under a sink, or water collecting around a shutoff valve. Others notice a wet cabinet base, a damp carpet edge near a wall, or a water meter that moves after every faucet and appliance has been turned off.

A hissing sound behind drywall can point to a pressurized water line, while a musty odor near a vanity or laundry wall can come from water that has sat in framing or insulation. Water around a fixture may also come from a loose supply connection, a worn seal, a cracked drain fitting, or a pipe joint farther behind the wall.

Those signs can look alike from the room, but the repair changes with the failed part and where the water has traveled. A visible valve connection, a pinhole in copper tubing, and a split fitting inside a wall require different materials, access work, and labor.

sections.heading: Leak inspection and pressure test
paragraphs: We begin the callout by checking the wet area, nearby fixtures, exposed supply lines, shutoff valves, and the water meter. We look for fresh water at joints, corrosion around valve stems, movement at compression fittings, and staining that shows the direction of the water path. We may also isolate a fixture or branch line before removing a cabinet panel or opening a small section of drywall.

We compare static and flowing water pressure, with residential plumbing commonly operating between 40 and 80 psi, and use the meter to help confirm ongoing water loss. A basic visible-area inspection and pressure check may take about 10 to 15 minutes before repair work begins. We replace accessible washers, supply lines, valve components, fittings, or damaged pipe sections during the visit when the part and access allow it; wall restoration, concealed pipe routing, or special-order parts may need a separate appointment.

sections.heading: Shutoff valves and wall access
paragraphs: The age and condition of the failed fitting affect the repair because older compression nuts, galvanized pipe, corroded copper, and brittle plastic connections can break or deform during removal. A shutoff valve that turns freely gives us a clean way to isolate one fixture, while a seized valve may require additional work at the branch line or main shutoff.

Access also changes the scope. A leak below an open sink cabinet usually gives us room for a wrench and replacement fitting, but a pipe behind tile, drywall, insulation, or a finished ceiling may require a careful opening to reach the joint. A matching valve cartridge, specialty fitting, or fixture-specific part that must be ordered can extend the repair beyond the first visit, and some pipe work may require inspection or sign-off before a wall closes.

sections.heading: Fixture model and wall access
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room has the leak and which fixture sits closest to the wet area, such as the upstairs bathtub, laundry washer box, kitchen sink, or bathroom vanity. If water comes from a faucet, valve, or appliance connection, check for a model number or make stamped on the fixture body, trim plate, supply hose, or appliance label. Tell us whether water is running now, dripping only after use, or showing up below the room where the fixture sits. Let us know whether the pipe is visible in a cabinet, crawl space, garage, or utility room, or hidden behind tile or drywall. Call BT Round Rock Plumbing at (737) 215-4933 before a leaking pipe keeps soaking the cabinet, ceiling, or wall framing.

services.name: Toilet Repair
services.h1: Toilet Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Toilet Repair | BT Round Rock Plumbing | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: BT Round Rock Plumbing handles toilet repair in Round Rock, TX, checking running tanks, weak flushes, leaks at the base, and failed fill valves on a callout.
services.blurb: Toilet repairs for running tanks, weak flushes, leaks, and loose handles in Round Rock.

paragraphs: Most people reach for a plunger first, and that makes sense when paper or waste has slowed the bowl. A few steady plunges can restore a normal flush without taking apart the tank or removing the toilet. The plunger stops helping when the blockage sits beyond the trapway, the water rises in the bowl, or the flush valve inside the tank no longer opens correctly.

We also see homeowners jiggle a loose handle, shorten a slack chain, or press down on a flapper that will not seal. Those small adjustments can stop a running tank for a while, but a worn rubber flapper, cracked overflow tube, or failing fill valve usually brings the sound back. Water that keeps entering the tank can run through the bowl long after the bathroom has gone quiet.

A toilet with a stiff handle or occasional weak flush can often wait for a planned repair visit if the bowl stays at its normal water level. Water spreading from the base, a bowl that threatens to overflow, or a tank that runs continuously should not wait, because the wax ring, flooring, and water bill can all worsen while the fixture keeps leaking.

sections.heading: Toilet keeps running
paragraphs: Customers often tell us the toilet keeps running, the tank will not fill, the handle does nothing, or the bowl will not flush all the way. A hissing tank can point to a fill valve that will not shut off, while water trickling into the bowl often points to a flapper or flush valve seal. A handle that moves freely without flushing can come from a broken lever arm, disconnected chain, or warped flapper.

Water around the toilet base, a rocking bowl, sewer-like odor near the floor, and gurgling after a flush need a different check from a running tank. A loose closet bolt, failed wax ring, blocked trapway, or damaged flange can create similar symptoms from outside the bowl. Each complaint can lead to a different part and a different amount of work, even when the sound or puddle looks much the same before we inspect it.

sections.heading: Toilet callout inspection
paragraphs: We start by flushing the toilet, watching the bowl level, and listening to the fill valve after the flush cycle ends. We remove the tank lid, check the handle, chain, flapper, overflow tube, and water line, then inspect the shutoff valve and supply connection. A standard tank check commonly takes about 15 to 30 minutes, depending on whether the bowl and base also need testing.

We use a dye test to find water slipping past the flapper, measure the tank water line against the overflow tube, and check the floor around the bowl for movement or moisture. A 2-inch or 3-inch flush valve needs the matching seal and flapper style, so we identify the fitting before replacing it. We also check whether the shutoff valve turns cleanly before disconnecting the supply tube.

Flappers, fill valves, handles, chains, and supply tubes can often be replaced during the same visit after we confirm the failed part. A toilet that needs to be pulled for a wax ring, flange repair, damaged subfloor, or seized shutoff may need a return visit, especially if the correct flange part or bowl-specific component has to be ordered. We test the flush, refill, and base after the repair before putting the tank lid back.

sections.heading: Fill valves and shutoffs
paragraphs: The age and condition of the fill valve, flapper, flush valve, and handle move the repair cost because a single worn tank part takes less work than several aging fittings. A corroded tank bolt, cracked overflow tube, or specialty flush assembly can add labor and require a part that matches the toilet model. A toilet with a standard replacement fitting usually stays simpler than a fixture with discontinued internal parts.

Access also matters around the toilet and behind the tank. A shutoff valve that has seized can turn a tank repair into a valve replacement, while a bowl that must be lifted can expose a damaged wax ring, flange, or floor. Parts that must be ordered, changes requiring a local sign-off, and tight bathroom access all add steps beyond a straightforward flapper or handle replacement.

sections.heading: Tank model and bowl location
paragraphs: Before calling, check which bathroom holds the toilet and whether water is running into the bowl right now. A photo of the tank interior, handle, flapper, and water level can help us identify the likely fitting before the visit. Look for the manufacturer name and model marking inside the tank, near the water line, or under the tank lid.

Let us know roughly when the toilet was installed, whether the bowl rocks on the floor, and whether water appears only after flushing. Clear the floor around the base and leave access to the shutoff valve behind the bowl if furniture or storage blocks it. Call BT Round Rock Plumbing at (737) 215-4933 before a base leak softens the flooring or a running tank continues sending water through the overflow tube.

services.name: Faucet Repair
services.h1: Faucet Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Faucet Repair | BT Round Rock Plumbing | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: BT Round Rock Plumbing repairs dripping, loose, leaking, and low-flow faucets in Round Rock, TX with cartridge, handle, aerator, and valve checks.
services.blurb: Faucet repair for drips, loose handles, leaks, and low flow in Round Rock.

paragraphs: We hear calls about a faucet that “won’t stop dripping,” a handle that “just spins,” or water that comes out around the base instead of the spout. We translate those descriptions into checks of the cartridge, stem, handle screw, aerator, O-rings, and supply connections. A kitchen faucet and a bathroom sink faucet can make the same sound while failing at different parts.

We work on faucets in Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch, starting with the fixture that is leaking or no longer controlling the water correctly. A drip from the spout can often wait for a planned repair, but water under the sink cabinet or from the faucet base should not wait because it can soak the cabinet floor, loosen countertop material, and damage the shutoff connections.

sections.heading: Dripping spout and loose handle
paragraphs: A steady drip from the spout after the handle is off often points to a worn cartridge, seat, washer, or seal inside the faucet body. A handle that turns too far, feels loose, or comes off in your hand can involve a stripped handle adapter, a missing set screw, or a worn stem. Water running from the handle area usually comes from a stem seal or cartridge O-ring rather than the spout.

A faucet that only delivers a trickle may have mineral buildup in the aerator, debris at the cartridge ports, or a partly closed shutoff valve beneath the sink. Water that sprays sideways from the spout can come from a split aerator screen or a damaged spray head. These symptoms can look similar from the counter, but each fault calls for different parts and different work once we inspect the fixture.

sections.heading: Faucet callout and inspection
paragraphs: We begin the callout by checking the faucet body, handle movement, spout, aerator, supply tubes, and the cabinet floor for active water. We run hot and cold water separately, inspect the shutoff valves, and check for seepage at the compression nuts and hose connections. A basic faucet inspection commonly takes about ten to twenty minutes before we know whether the problem sits in the cartridge, handle, aerator, or supply line.

After isolating the water at the shutoff valves, we remove the handle and trim, identify the cartridge or stem, and inspect the seals and retaining clip. Replacing an accessible cartridge, aerator, O-ring, or handle screw often fits into the same visit and commonly takes about thirty to ninety minutes once the correct part is on hand. A seized shutoff valve, a discontinued cartridge, corrosion inside the faucet body, or a fixture that must be removed from the countertop can require a return visit after parts are obtained.

sections.heading: Cartridge age and shutoff valves
paragraphs: Cartridge age and faucet design affect the repair because many manufacturers use different stems, clips, seals, and handle adapters across faucet lines. A common cartridge that we can identify from the faucet body usually keeps the repair straightforward, while an older or discontinued cartridge may need to be ordered. A faucet with corrosion around the retaining nut can also take more labor to open without damaging the body.

Shutoff valves and cabinet access matter before we can reach the cartridge. Working valves beneath an open sink cabinet allow us to isolate the fixture cleanly, while seized stops, packed cabinets, or a supply tube pressed against the wall add work around the repair. If the job expands beyond the faucet into an alteration that requires a permit or sign-off, we discuss that requirement before proceeding.

sections.heading: Model number and fixture room
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room contains the faucet and whether it serves a kitchen sink, bathroom sink, laundry sink, bar sink, or tub. We can use the brand name, handle shape, and a clear photo of the spout and trim to narrow down the cartridge or adapter. Look for a model number on the installation sheet, receipt, original box, or tag under the sink if one is available. Tell us roughly how old the faucet is and whether water is dripping now, leaking into the cabinet, or only failing when the handle moves. Clear enough space around the sink cabinet for us to reach the shutoff valves and supply hoses. Call BT Round Rock Plumbing at (737) 215-4933 before water at the faucet base keeps reaching the cabinet floor or countertop seam.

services.name: Sewer Line Repair
services.h1: Sewer Line Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Sewer Line Repair | BT Round Rock Plumbing | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: BT Round Rock Plumbing handles sewer line repair in Round Rock, TX, with camera inspection, pipe repair planning, excavation, and clear scope notes.
services.blurb: Camera inspections and sewer line repairs for Round Rock-area properties.

paragraphs: Older homes and properties with aging cast-iron, clay, or early plastic pipe can develop sewer trouble below the yard, slab, or driveway. Around Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch, tree roots, shifting soil, separated joints, and worn pipe walls can stop wastewater from reaching the municipal connection. We trace the line from the cleanout toward the blockage or damaged section before recommending a repair.

A sewer line problem should not wait once wastewater backs up, a toilet bubbles during a shower, or sewage reaches a floor drain. Continued use sends more water through a damaged pipe, which can spread sewage into a bathroom, laundry room, or yard and make the affected section harder to reach safely. We inspect the pipe route and help determine what needs repair before the backup causes further damage.

sections.heading: Sewage odor and gurgling drains
paragraphs: Customers often call after hearing gurgling from a toilet while the washing machine drains, seeing water rise in a tub, or finding a floor drain that will not clear. A sewage odor near a cleanout, bathroom, or side yard can also point to a cracked sewer pipe, an open joint, or a blocked line. Slow drainage throughout several fixtures differs from one sink that drains slowly because the restriction may sit farther down the main line.

Water may appear at the cleanout cap, around a toilet base, or in the lowest shower or tub first because those openings sit closest to the sewer line. Roots inside a clay joint, a collapsed pipe wall, a low section holding solids, and a blockage at the connection can produce similar sounds and backups. Each fault calls for different materials, access work, and repair scope, so the cause needs a camera view or line test before anyone can sort out the likely cost.

sections.heading: Camera inspection and line locating
paragraphs: We begin the visit at the accessible cleanout and check which fixtures trigger the backup, where water appears, and whether the cap, riser, or drain opening provides a usable entry point. A camera inspection commonly takes about 30 to 60 minutes, depending on the pipe route, standing water, and amount of debris in the line. We watch for root intrusion, offset joints, cracks, bellies, and changes between cast iron, clay, ABS, and PVC pipe.

We measure the line route from the cleanout, identify the approximate damaged area, and note whether the pipe is commonly 3 or 4 inches in diameter. On a suitable first visit, we can inspect the line, locate the trouble area, and explain the repair path. Excavation, replacement of a buried section, utility marking, and any required permit or inspection are normally scheduled after the pipe route and access conditions have been confirmed.

sections.heading: Pipe depth and yard access
paragraphs: The material and condition of the buried pipe affect the repair scope. A cracked clay section, corroded cast-iron pipe, separated coupling, or crushed plastic line may require a different replacement method and different fittings. A line that has failed at several joints can also change the decision from replacing one section to addressing a longer run.

Access around the pipe route matters just as much as the break itself. A cleanout beside an open side yard gives a different excavation path than a line below a driveway, patio, landscaping bed, slab edge, or fence. Utility locations, a seized cleanout cap, a section that needs special-order pipe or couplings, and city sign-off requirements can add steps before the repair can be completed.

sections.heading: Cleanout location and pipe material
paragraphs: Before calling, check where the cleanout sits and whether it is in the front yard, side yard, garage, bathroom, or near the foundation. Note which fixtures back up first, whether sewage or water is running out now, and whether the problem occurs when a toilet flushes, a shower drains, or the washing machine discharges. If an earlier repair left a cap, receipt, camera report, or pipe material note, keep it available for the visit.

A clear photo of the cleanout and the surrounding fence, driveway, shrubs, or concrete can help us plan access to the pipe route. Let us know if a gate stays locked, a vehicle blocks the cleanout, or a pet uses the yard where excavation may be needed. Call BT Round Rock Plumbing at (737) 215-4933 before a sewer backup spreads from the drain opening into flooring, walls, or the yard.
